Pontificate

pon-TIF-ih-kayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To pontificate is to pompously express opinions.

Every Sunday dinner, Uncle Ray would pontificate about politics as though his opinion were simply beyond question.

Worked Example

At every family dinner, Grandpa would pontificate about the state of modern music as though no one could possibly disagree.

It wasn't just that he shared an opinion -- it was the pompous certainty and length of it, as if disagreement were unthinkable, that makes this pontificating.

How Pontificate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

lecture

lecture: to talk at someone in a scolding or instructive way

hold forth

hold forth: to speak at length, often about one's own views

Antonyms

defer

defer: to yield to someone else's judgment

How Strong Is It? — opine → pontificate → harangue

opine vs. pontificate

opine vs. pontificate: To opine is simply to state an opinion; to pontificate is to do so pompously, at length, as though the matter were settled.

harangue vs. pontificate

harangue vs. pontificate: A harangue goes further still, becoming a forceful, scolding speech rather than just a self-important opinion.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pontific

root — pontific: high priest (Latin (pontifex))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Pontific- (from pontifex, the Latin title for Rome's high priest) plus the verb-forming -ate gives 'to act the high priest' -- to pontificate is to talk as if you held that same unquestionable religious authority.

Use the root in a new word: pontiff

Use the root in a new word: pontiff: Pontiff is the modern English title drawn from the very same Latin word for a high priest, now used for the pope.
